activities.title: Clap the parts of names
parentPrompts: Say your child's name slowly and clap once for each part. For "Ma-ri-a" that is three claps.
Clap the names of family members, pets, and favorite toys. After each one, ask: "How many claps?"
Take turns: they pick a name, you clap it. Then switch, and let them check you.
Challenge: say a word in parts, like "pic-nic," and see if they can say the whole word.

activities.title: Build your name with letters
materials: playdough or magnetic letters or letter cards
parentPrompts: Write your child's name in big capital letters on an index card, starting with a capital and using lowercase for the rest.
Point to each letter and name it. Ask them to touch each one as you say it again.
Let them copy the name with playdough ropes or letter pieces, matching each letter to the card.
Ask: "Which letter does your name start with?" Then look for that letter on signs, boxes, or books during the day.

activities.title: Find things that start like my name
parentPrompts: Say the first sound of your child's name, not the letter name. For "Mia" say "mmm," keeping the sound short and clean.
Find 3 to 5 things around the house that start with that sound and put them in the basket.
Hold each one up and stretch its first sound: "mmmmug." Let them say it with you.
Make a silly sentence together using that sound, like "Mighty Mia makes music."

activities.title: Rhyme with names
parentPrompts: Ask: "Does Sam rhyme with ham?" then "Does Sam rhyme with dog?" Let them decide yes or no.
Make rhymes for names in the family. Nonsense words are fine, because the goal is hearing the matching ending.
Take turns: you say a name, they say something that rhymes, then switch.
Sing or say a rhyming song or nursery rhyme you both know and pause before the rhyming word.

activities.title: Read a book about feelings or families
materials: a picture book about feelings or families
parentPrompts: Read the book once for fun, with expression. Pause to look at the pictures.
On a second look, ask: "How is this character feeling? How can you tell?"
Ask: "Have you ever felt like that? What happened?"
Ask them to tell you their favorite part in their own words.

activities.title: Count fingers, toes, and more
parentPrompts: Count fingers on one hand, touching each one as you say the number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Then the other hand.
Count toes the same way, then eyes, ears, and noses. Ask: "How many do you have?"
After counting, say the last number again: "Five fingers on this hand." This shows that the last number tells how many.
Hold up some fingers and ask them to count them. Then ask them to show you 3 fingers, then 4.

subject: math
title: How many letters in my name?

activities.title: Count and compare the letters in names
materials: index cards with names written on them
parentPrompts: Write your child's name on a card and put one counter on each letter. Count the counters together.
Do the same for a family member. Line up the two rows of counters side by side.
Ask: "Whose name has more? Whose has fewer? Do any have the same?"
Try a pet or a friend. Keep small counters out of mouths and stay close while they play.

activities.title: Make a group for each number
materials: index cards with the numerals 1 to 5 written on them
parentPrompts: Lay out the number cards in order and say each number.
Hold up a card and ask them to build a group with that many blocks. Count the group together to check.
Mix up the cards. Ask: "Can you show me 3?" and let them make the group and find the card.
Play a quick game: you make a group, they find the card that matches.

activities.title: Sort shoes (or socks or toy cars)
materials: a pile of shoes, socks, or toy cars
parentPrompts: Dump out the pile and ask: "How could we put these in groups?"
Sort them one way, such as by color or by shoes with laces and shoes without. Let them place each one.
Ask: "How are the ones in this group the same? How are they different from that group?"
Mix them up and sort a different way. Notice that the same things can be grouped in more than one way.

activities.title: Make patterns with your body
parentPrompts: Start a pattern with your body: clap, stomp, clap, stomp. Ask: "What comes next?"
Let them keep the pattern going while you join in. Say the pattern out loud together.
Take turns inventing patterns: tap-tap-clap, tap-tap-clap, or jump-touch your head.
Copy a body pattern with blocks: clap becomes a red block and stomp becomes a blue one.

activities.title: Decorate the letters of your name
materials: scraps of colored paper or old magazines
parentPrompts: Write your child's name in big outline letters on the paper.
Let them tear or cut scraps and glue them inside the letters, however they like.
Talk while they work: "What colors are you using? Which letter are you working on?"
When done, ask them to tell you about their picture and hang it up.

activities.title: Draw faces for different feelings
parentPrompts: Draw a happy face together, then ask: "What does a sad face look like? A silly face? An angry one?"
Let them draw each feeling on a plate. Talk about what changes in the face.
Ask: "When do you feel happy? When do you feel mad?"
Ask: "What helps when we feel upset?" Practice one idea together, like deep breaths or a hug.

activities.title: Turn handprints into people or animals
materials: a tray or plate for paint
parentPrompts: Spread a thin layer of paint on a tray. Help them press a hand and then press it on paper.
Once it is dry, draw on it: a face and legs make a person, and fingers can become a tree or an octopus.
Count the fingers in the handprint together.
Ask them to name their creation and tell you something about it.

activities.title: Trace and decorate a body outline
parentPrompts: Have them lie on the paper while you trace around their body.
Let them add a face, hair, and clothes with crayons.
Point to a body part and ask them to name it, or name one and ask them to point: "Where are your elbows?"
Hang it up. Ask: "What can your hands do? What can your feet do?"

activities.title: Draw the people in your family
parentPrompts: Invite them to draw the people in their family, or whoever they live with and love. Any way they draw is fine.
Ask them to tell you about each person: "What does this person like to do?"
Write the names next to the people as they say them, and have them point to the first letter.
Count the people in the picture together.
